label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
**The busing project, or why I'm not dropping it**

Some of you know a parent complained about the oral history project I give my juniors. A few of you have already seen the short version in the group chat, and the reaction was mostly "it's one assignment, is it worth your job?" Jess, that's basically what you said. I'd rather answer properly here than in fifteen texts that go nowhere. You're not wrong that I could get burned. I just don't think you're seeing what the assignment actually is.

Here's the project. US History II, two sections of juniors. Each kid interviews someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston in 1974 to 1976, when busing and desegregation tore through the city. They record a ten-minute interview and write a two-page reflection. I've run it for four years at Cobb Street, and nobody has ever complained until now.

This year a parent emailed the principal, Dr. Halvorsen, and copied a school committee member. Her main points were that the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." I read that email several times. Honestly, I think she has a point about the second part. Judging your grandparents is a lot to ask of a fifteen-year-old, and I've never wanted a kid to walk into a family's kitchen looking for a villain. I'm not picking a fight with her. I have a meeting with her and Dr. Halvorsen on Thursday, November 19, at 3:15, and I plan to go in listening.

What I'm not going to do is quietly drop it. Here's why.

A couple of years ago, a kid I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother. She had driven a school bus in South Boston in '74, and she had never told anyone in the family about it, not in any real detail. D. played about forty seconds of the recording for the class, and nobody said a word for close to a minute. I've thought about that minute a lot. It was the most honest silence I've ever been part of in a classroom.

Last year a girl found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus when he was a teenager. She was upset, and she should have been. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year, and not because it had a neat ending. It was because she was working out, on paper, what it means to love someone and also be ashamed of what they did. That's exactly the thinking I want from them.

Those are the kids this project is for. The ones who are uncomfortable are often the ones who most need it, because it may be the only place in their schooling where their own family's history gets a serious hearing. Textbooks give this period about one paragraph. For kids who live in this city, that's not a small omission. It's the history of the streets they walk to school on.

So here's my plan for Thursday, and why I think it's fair. I keep the project and add an alternate option. A kid who doesn't want to interview family can interview a librarian or archivist, or use recorded interviews from past years, with permission from the people in them. No student is required to sit across from a relative and ask about something painful. That's the line I'm drawing. I don't get to force anyone. I do get to build a version of the assignment that's honest about the history without making anyone a participant against their will.

Now, Jess. I know why you said what you said. You remember us student teaching together in 2012, and you watched me get excited about lesson plans at eleven at night. You left teaching in 2019 and now do HR at a biotech in Cambridge, and I think part of you looked at this and thought, she's going to get hurt over something that doesn't feel worth it. That's a kind thing to think. I'm not asking you to agree with me. I'm asking you to understand that I'm not doing this because I'm brave. I'm a little scared. I've been tenured since 2021, which helps, but Halvorsen still controls my schedule and who gets AP sections, and I know that. I'm doing it anyway because the alternative is deciding that the kids who most need this work don't get it, and I'm not willing to make that call for them.

If this were a lesson on something harmless, I'd drop it in a second. Nobody gets a medal for defending a bad assignment. But this is the history of the place they live. Pretending it didn't happen, or only teaching it through one textbook paragraph, is also a choice, and it's one made on their behalf.

I'm not writing this to win anything. I wanted to explain myself once, clearly, to people whose opinions I trust, including the ones who think I'm overreacting. If you think the alternate option is wrong, tell me. If you have a better idea for handling the second half of that parent's email, I want to hear it. I'd rather get a useful argument than a pile of "be careful" texts.

Thursday after the meeting, I'll text you. Good news or bad. You'll be the first to know, which feels right, since you're the one I've been arguing with in my head all week.

---

A few notes before you post:

- You might not want to name Dr. Halvorsen or the parent on a blog, even a small one. Consider "my principal" and "a parent." Naming them could make the meeting harder, and it's easy to change.
- The D. story and the uncle story are anonymized, but in a school community people may guess who they're about. Check that you're comfortable with the level of detail, especially the grandmother's job and the South Boston detail.

reasons: The appended notes address the user rather than belonging to the blog post, so the piece does not end with warmth toward Jess and shifts out of the teacher’s persona.
